articles.summary: What Problem Does CXL MRAM Solve in the Data Center? stephanie.quinn Thu, 19 Nov 2026 - 08:53 Click Here to Read PDF Version Image MRAM has been solving persistent-write problems in enterprise storage for years. CXL gives us a way to bring that same persistence much closer to the processor. That is what makes this interesting. Everspin has already demonstrated CXL-attached DDR4 MRAM using an FPGA-based CXL platform and Everspin MRAM DIMMs. The platform passed memory stress and stability testing, including Google’s stress application used to demonstrate memory stability in enterprise environments. Now we want to move beyond basic platform validation and put customer-relevant workloads on it. The question we are trying to answer is straightforward: How much can system performance improve when CPUs, GPUs and other accelerators spend less time waiting on storage? How is CXL different from NVMe? Both CXL and NVMe use PCIe as the physical transport, but they were designed around different jobs. NVMe was optimized around storage. CXL was designed to support memory and processor/accelerator attachment, too. For MRAM, that opens up a different way to connect into systems. With an NVMe SSD, write-access latency is typically measured in hundred of microseconds. With CXL-attached MRAM, the MRAM write plus the CXL interface latency can be measured in hundreds of nanoseconds. From an access-latency perspective, you are moving persistent storage much closer to the DRAM domain. The goal is to reduce the time processors spend waiting for storage to complete an operation so they can spend more time doing useful work. If that translates into higher XPU utilization, the value goes beyond performance. It means getting more productive work from expensive compute infrastructure, which can improve both CapEx and OpEx. Is Power Loss Really a Concern in a Data Center? That question comes up frequently. The first reaction is often, “We have backup power. Why do I care?” Because losing utility power is only one way volatile data disappears. A server can crash. A system can reboot. If important information exists only in DRAM at that point, it is gone. The traditional answer is checkpointing. Move the important information out of DRAM and into storage so it can be recovered after restart. Now you are back to the storage path and its latency. Battery-backed DRAM takes another approach. Keep the DRAM alive long enough to move its contents into NAND when power fails. It works, but that means DRAM, a battery-backed unit, NAND and the circuitry and software needed to make the transfer happen correctly when something has already gone wrong, with the looming risk of a battery failure. MRAM changes that part of the architecture because the data is already persistent once the write completes. Where does CXL MRAM fit in the Memory Hierarchy? We do not see this primarily as a component-replacement story. MRAM in many of these use cases is not a component displacement. It is a system solution. The CPU still needs DRAM. DRAM remains closely coupled to the processor because of its performance, bandwidth and capacity characteristics. NAND is not going away either. It remains extremely effective for storing very large amounts of data at low cost. CXL MRAM adds a persistent tier for data that needs much lower write latency than the storage path can provide. One use case is a persistent write buffer or cache in front of NAND. DRAM can continue serving the workloads where volatile memory is acceptable. NAND remains the large-capacity compute storage layer. MRAM handles selected persistent data where small writes, latency or recovery are becoming bottlenecks. That is also why comparing MRAM and NAND strictly on dollars per gigabyte can lead you in the wrong direction. They are solving different problems in the system. Small Writes are Where this Gets Interesting Small writes can create a disproportionate amount of pain in a storage system. NAND is very effective for high-capacity storage, but small payloads are harder to handle efficiently unless they are accumulated first. That adds latency exactly where applications with lots of small writes can least afford it. MRAM is particularly interesting when you have many small pieces of persistent data changing frequently. Transactional databases are one example. Metadata is another. Key-value cache activity and other small data structures can create similar behavior. Everspin has already been serving data center storage applications for 15 years. MRAM has been used for journal memory, persistent buffering, metadata and computational storage. IBM FlashCore, for example, uses MRAM for metadata, consistency data, redirection tables, telemetry and other small pieces of information that are important to how the storage subsystem operates. CXL builds on that history by giving persistent MRAM another way to connect closer to the processor. Which Workloads Benefit Most from CXL MRAM? The honest answer is that it depends on the workload. The more frequent the writes, the smaller the writes and the greater the write latency sensitivity the more interesting the opportunity becomes. From there, the details matter. How large are the writes? How often do they occur? Is the processor spending time waiting for persistent storage? Is storage performance limiting the rest of the system? And how much low-latency persistent memory would it take to change that? Those are the questions that determine whether CXL MRAM can make a meaningful difference. That lets the small-writes section explain the technology and examples, while the workload section helps the customer determine whether they have the problem. How Much CXL MRAM does a System Really Need? Potentially much less than people assume. One of the easiest mistakes to make is starting the conversation with the price of MRAM per gigabyte and comparing it directly with NAND. That misses the architecture discussion as it is not one or the other – they create greater value together. In one IBM FlashCore configuration, 256 MB of MRAM supports up to 100 TB of NAND storage. You do not need MRAM to replace terabytes of storage to change how the system behaves. IBM is using MRAM where persistence, write performance and latency create enough value to justify that portion of the architecture. That is a much more useful way to think about CXL MRAM. Instead of asking how much MRAM you can put in a server, ask: How much persistent, low-latency memory does this workload actually need? What about Endurance? This was one of the tougher questions and it is one we should be asking. If MRAM is used as a cache and the architecture continually writes the same location, endurance matters. You cannot brute-force the device and assume memory technology makes the engineering problem disappear. Existing deployments have had to engineer around this too. Data placement, leveling and workload management all matter. IBM faced the same issue in its persistent-memory architecture and designed the system around the endurance available from the memory. A generic endurance number tells you one thing. Understanding where the writes occur, how frequently they occur and how the data moves through the system tells you whether the architecture works. Is this a New, Unproven Memory Technology? No. The new part is the CXL connection, not MRAM’s role in enterprise storage. Everspin’s demonstration takes a memory technology already proven in data-center storage and exposes it through CXL, bringing persistent MRAM closer to CPUs, GPUs and other processors. The platform shows that the concept works. The next question is where it creates the most value. Transactional databases? Metadata? Checkpointing? AI infrastructure? Another workload where small, persistent writes are holding the system back? We do not want to guess. Bring us the Workload We have a working CXL MRAM platform. The next useful step is not another generic benchmark. It is putting workloads on it that represent real problems customers are trying to solve. Where are the small writes? What information needs to survive a server crash or restart? Are CPUs or GPUs waiting on persistent storage? How much persistent memory would change that? Those are the conversations we want to have. Bring us your workload. Let’s measure it.

articles.summary: The arena lights drop, the crowd counts down, and the first truck fires its engine on the floor below your seats. Your five-year-old grabs your arm with both hands and presses her face into your sleeve. Two rows down, another parent cups his palms over his toddler's ears, and he keeps them there through the whole opening run. Monster Jam ear protection should be on every person in your family, from the toddler on your lap to you. The concessions at each show sell some hearing protection, but bringing your own lets you check the fit and the rating before the first engine starts. AXIL makes officially licensed Monster Jam hearing protection, and the same fit and rating advice applies whichever brand your family ends up wearing. Question Quick answer How loud is Monster Jam? Average crowd levels at an indoor monster truck show measured in the high 90s dBA, with peaks above 120 dBA Do adults need ear protection? Yes, adults need ear protection as much as the kids do Does Monster Jam sell ear protection? Concessions sell novelty ear protection and disposable earplugs while supplies last Can you bring your own? Yes, Monster Jam allows ear protection brought from home What should toddlers and young kids wear? Snug earmuffs sized for small heads What should older kids and adults wear? Earplugs, earmuffs, or both for seats close to the floor How Loud Is Monster Jam Indoors and in Stadiums? Monster Jam gets loud enough to call for ear protection in both indoor arenas and outdoor stadiums. The clearest measurements come from an indoor show. When NIOSH researchers measured noise at an indoor monster truck show, average spectator levels ran from about 97 to 100 A-weighted decibels (dBA). Hearing damage risk starts at 85 dBA, and NIOSH advises protecting your hearing any time sound reaches that level. You can learn more about how that line was set in our guide to the 85 dB threshold. Indoor Arenas Hold Monster Jam Noise In An indoor arena's roof and walls hold sound in, so engine noise bounces around the bowl instead of escaping. The high-90s dBA average from the NIOSH study comes from this kind of venue, so it applies most directly to arena shows. Revving engines, big-air jumps, and crashes add sudden sound peaks on top of the steady sound of an engine roar. In the arena NIOSH measured, those peaks passed 120 dBA at every measurement spot. Stadium Seats Close to the Floor Still Take the Most Noise An open-air stadium gives sound more room to spread out, and sound gets lower the farther it travels from the trucks. Sitting in the upper-deck seats at a stadium can be easier on your ears than seats in the lower rows. Seats close to the floor are too near the engines of Monster Trucks. If your family is in the lower rows at a stadium show, plan on ear protection just as you would in an arena. How Long Monster Jam Noise Takes to Reach a Full Day's Sound Limit Monster Jam can reach NIOSH's full-day noise limit in 15 to 30 minutes. The NIOSH exposure chart cuts the safe listening time in half for every 3 dB above 85 dBA, which allows 30 minutes at 97 dBA and only 15 minutes at 100 dBA. A Monster Jam show runs about two hours, and a Pit Party adds more time on the arena floor before the show starts. Those two hours of noise reach every seat in your row. Do You Need Ear Protection at Monster Jam? Yes, every person at Monster Jam needs ear protection, from the toddler on your lap to the grandparent at the end of the row. That includes the adults who are busy protecting the kids. Adults Need Ear Protection as Much as Kids Adult ears take in the same high-90s dBA as kids' ears. A parent who buys earmuffs for the kids and skips a pair for themselves still sits through that same noise level for the next two hours with their ears unprotected. What Happens to Your Ears Without Protection If you experience ringing in your ears or muffled hearing on the drive home, those are signs that your ears took in more noise than they could handle. Hearing loss from noise exposure can be temporary, and your hearing may return to normal within 16 to 48 hours. But repeated exposure to loud sounds can add up over the years. articles.summary: If you've ever looked down at your kid mid-show and wondered, is it too loud in here? Trust that instinct, because it's usually right. And most parents never think to ask. The show that feels loud to you is louder for your kid. It's simple physics, and it has an easy fix. Concerts, Monster Jam, fireworks, race day at the track. Each one crosses into ear damaging territory, and each calls for something a little different: Event Recommended Protection Concerts & festivals Muffs (under 6) or MONSTER JAM earplugs (6+) Monster Jam Muffs (under 6) or MONSTER JAM earplugs (6+) Fireworks Muffs, plus distance from the launch site Stadium games Muffs (under 6) or MONSTER JAM earplugs (6+) Shooting range AXIL ear muffs over plugs, doubled up Kids Need More Hearing Protection Than Adults Do A child's ear canal is smaller and still developing, which raises the sound pressure hitting the eardrum at the exact same decibel level an adult standing right next to them is experiencing. Same show, same seat, harder hit. The Damage Is Cumulative and Permanent Every loud event adds to a running total a child's ears carry for life. Loud noise damages the tiny hair cells inside the cochlea, and unlike a scraped knee, those cells never heal or regenerate. The damage builds up show by show with no outward sign, and a child rarely complains about it the way they'd complain about anything else that hurts. But the damage can show up years later, long after anyone remembers the events that caused it. 85 Decibels Is the Threshold to Know None of that is meant to scare you off the next family outing. The number to know is 85 decibels (dB), the point where unprotected exposure time starts counting against a child's hearing, according to the CDC and NIDCD. Concerts, Monster Jam, fireworks: most clear that threshold within minutes of the gates opening. A little preparation goes a long way. Watch for This One Warning Sign If your child is covering their ears or telling you it's too loud, they've already crossed the safe limit. Treat that as your cue to have protection on before the show starts. You know the 85-decibel limit sits. Next is how fast the events on your family's calendar reach it. How Loud Are Kids' Events? Here's the Decibel Breakdown Monster Jam, concerts, fireworks, stadium games, air shows: all of it clears that 85 dB line, some by a wide margin. Fireworks alone can peak more than 60 decibels above it at close range. Decibel Levels by Event Event Typical Level Peak Level Safe Exposure Time* Movie theaters 75–85 dB 90–100 dB (action scenes) Hours typical; ~15 min during loud scenes Stadium games 94–110 dB Up to 142 dB (crowd roar) ~2–60 min Concerts & festivals 100–110 dB N/A ~2–15 min Monster Jam 95–100 dB 120+ dB ~15–45 min Motorsport grandstands 100–115 dB N/A ~30 sec–15 min Air shows 110–120 dB N/A ~10 sec–2 min Fireworks (close range) N/A 140–150 dB Seconds These exposure times reflect NIOSH's 3-decibel exchange rate (every 3 dB increase cuts safe exposure roughly in half), applied across each event's dB range, from CDC/NIOSH. Exact figures vary by venue, seating, and speaker placement. Do Kids Need Ear Protection at Loud Events? Yes. Anything that holds 85 dB for a sustained stretch qualifies, and that covers nearly everything on your family's calendar this year. The fix from here is simple: match the protection to your kid's age first, then fine-tune for the event. The Right Ear Protection Changes as Your Kid Grows Here’s a trusty rule of thumb for your kid’s ear protection: ear muffs win for kids under about 6, earplugs take over from there. If you've ever tried to keep an earplug seated in a toddler's ear for more than ninety seconds, you already know why. Muffs never go into the canal, so there's nothing to insert wrong, and you can check the fit at a glance without asking a toddler to hold still (good luck with that). A toddler also can't yank off a pair of muffs one-handed the way they can pop out a plug the second you look away. Earplugs become realistic once a child can seat one properly and tell you if something's off. For most kids, that's right around age 6.
